note: Promotion to the tracked schema (roadmap Phase 1 backfill). Track groups follow the (XX) prefixes already embedded in the source theme names; only empty fields are filled.

themes.description: Supporting the head, the safe carries and the safe sleep position — handling an infant with confidence.
The short list behind crying — hunger, wind, tiredness, discomfort — worked through in order before despair.
How infants are fed and the practicalities of each — hunger cues, hygiene, and support for the person feeding.
What infant sleep actually looks like, the safe sleep rules, and surviving the nights as a household.

themes.theme: Talking to somebody who cannot talk back (IN)
themes.description: Why narration, songs and responses build a brain — serving conversation before there are words.

themes.theme: When a parent is not coping (IN)
themes.description: Exhaustion and low mood after a baby — the signs, the words to use, and the help that exists.
What play does for development at each stage, and playing with a baby using what a home already has.
What vaccines do, the schedule where you live, and answering a worried question with the evidence.

themes.theme: The home that is safe enough (IN)
themes.description: The hazards at a crawling child's height — water, heat, poisons, falls — found and fixed room by room.
What an older child can genuinely do for a baby, and the jobs that stay with adults.
The ordinary range of growing up — bodies, moods, abilities — and the changes worth a professional look.

themes.theme: A child who is struggling at school (CH)
themes.description: Reading the signs behind falling behind — sight, hearing, home, bullying — before concluding laziness.
What screens give and take at each age, and household rules that are followed because they are fair.
How friendships form and fail through childhood, and helping a lonely child without engineering their life.

themes.theme: The body a teenager is getting used to (CH)
themes.description: Puberty as it actually unfolds — timing, variation, feelings — and being askable when questions come.
Why adolescents seek risk, the difference between growth risks and harm, and steering without forbidding everything.
When trouble arrives — school, police, substances — the adult response that helps in the first 24 hours.
First earnings and spending — helping a teenager run real money with real mistakes at a survivable size.
The skills audit before independence — cooking, money, paperwork — and the leaving that keeps the door open.
Giving a young person genuine responsibility — sized to stretch, supervised lightly, and owned by them.
The checks and symptoms adults defer — and the short list that should never wait for a quiet month.

themes.theme: Working with a body that hurts (AD)
themes.description: Working life with pain — pacing, adjustments and the difference between soreness and damage.

themes.theme: Being the person everybody depends on (AD)
themes.description: Carrying a household, a job and other people's needs — the load named honestly and shared deliberately.

themes.theme: A partner, a household, a plan (AD)
themes.description: Running a shared life on purpose — money, work, care and the conversations that keep them agreed.
Job loss handled in order — money triage, entitlements, the search — and the identity blow named as real.

themes.theme: The friend who has stopped answering (AD)
themes.description: Noticing withdrawal in an adult friend and reaching them without ambush or retreat.
What grief does to a person and a household, what helps, and the support that fits each age.
The documents an adult life runs on — ID, insurance, wills, records — organised so someone else could find them.
Retraining and starting again mid-life — the routes that exist, the costs, and the transferable skills already held.

themes.theme: Being somebody a young person can call (AD)
themes.description: Mentoring without a program — being a safe, steady adult a young person can actually reach.
What ordinary ageing changes — strength, senses, speed — and what is illness rather than age.
Why falls end independence, the home hazards behind most of them, and the strength work that prevents them.
The adaptations, services and routines that keep an older person safely in their own home longer.
Ordinary forgetting versus concerning change, the assessment path, and living well alongside dementia.
What isolation does to health, and the contact — visits, calls, groups — that measurably protects.
Pensions, entitlements and the scams aimed at older people — later-life money protected and claimed.
Receiving care while keeping choice and privacy — what dignity in care concretely requires.
Raising driving, safely and kindly, with evidence — and the alternatives that keep a life mobile.
Drawing out and recording the skills and stories an older person holds before they are lost.
Working past pension age — the rights, the adjustments and the roles where experience outweighs speed.
Recognising yourself as a carer — the role named, the entitlements it unlocks, and the support registered for.
Moving a person safely for both of you — technique, aids and the moves never done alone.
Managing another person's medicines — schedule, storage, records — and the errors the system must prevent.

themes.theme: The carer who is not sleeping (CR)
themes.description: Care that breaks the carer's nights — the risks of running empty and the fixes worth fighting for.
Breaks that actually restore — arranging cover you trust and taking the time without guilt.

themes.theme: Caring for somebody who does not want it (CR)
themes.description: Refusal, pride and risk — caring within another adult's right to decide, and when safety overrides.
What dying looks like, what comfort care does, and being present in the last days without panic.
The first week's duties — certification, notification, the funeral — and the support for the person left.
Paid care as skilled work — the training, the standards and the routes into it locally.
The carer's own health, network and plan — kept deliberately, because the caring depends on it.
